references.text: The preceding dialogue where Jesus himself confesses his identity as the Messiah and Son of God, which leads the Council to conclude that they need no further witnesses ([ref:Luk 22:67-70|Luke 22:67-70]).
Matthew's parallel account where the high priest tears his clothes and says that they have now heard the blasphemy and need no more witnesses ([ref:Matt 26:65|Matthew 26:65]).
Mark's parallel account where the high priest tears his clothes and asks what further witnesses they need, having heard the blasphemy from Jesus' own mouth ([ref:Mark 14:63-64|Mark 14:63-64]).
The Jews accuse Jesus of blasphemy because he, being a man, makes himself God – the same accusation that underlies the Council's verdict in [ref:Joh 10:33|John 10:33].

The Jews explain to Pilate that according to their law Jesus must die because he has made himself the Son of God – a direct consequence of what the Council heard from Jesus' own mouth ([ref:Joh 19:7|John 19:7]).

The Mosaic Law requires two or three witnesses to impose a death sentence, but here the Council considers Jesus' own words sufficient to make further testimony unnecessary ([ref:5 Mos 17:6|Deuteronomy 17:6]).

The law's requirement that a case must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses – the Council regards Jesus' own statement as sufficient evidence ([ref:5 Mos 19:15|Deuteronomy 19:15]).
Stephen was also accused of blasphemy based on testimony about what he had said, with a parallel to the accusation against Jesus ([ref:Apg 6:11-14|Acts 6:11-14]).
